_doc: How this framework spells the agnostic vocabulary. The canon — which axes exist, their canonical values, the anti-synonym glossary — lives in @ds/contracts/prop-canon.json and is framework-free. This file holds ONLY the places Angular's idiom differs from it.
_why: A contract says a component has a selection that can be controlled. It does not say whether that is `value` + `onValueChange`, `modelValue` + `update:modelValue`, or `[(value)]`, because that is a framework's business and not the specification's. Three backends now spell it three ways and the contract was not edited for any of them.

conventions.propCase: camelCase. Angular does not normalise case in templates the way Vue does, so a `readOnly` input is written `[readOnly]` and NOT `read-only`. This is the one place a consumer moving between the Vue and Angular builds must change what they type.
conventions.eventPrefix: none on the declaring side. A `model()` produces an output named `<X>Change`, which is what makes `[(X)]` work; `output()` would be used for anything else.
conventions.booleanNaming: bare adjective, as the canon requires. Angular needs no deviation.

_selectorDoc: THE FIELD WITH NO COUNTERPART IN THE OTHER TWO BACKENDS. An Angular component does not render its own root element; it ATTACHES to one chosen by its selector. So a binding's `element` compiles here into an attribute selector rather than into markup, and a consumer writes the element themselves.

selectorRule.note: The alternative — an element selector like `ds-button` — was rejected and the reason is not taste. It would make the host a custom element, and a <ds-button> is not a button: no native focus, no native `disabled`, no implicit role, no form participation. @ds/platform-web records all four as facts about `button`, and a backend that quietly discarded them would be compiling a different component from the same contract. It would also break the shared stylesheet, because the theme file dresses the element the contract named.
selectorRule.cost: A consumer types more than in React or Vue, and for a `div`-rooted component (`<div dsAccordion>`) it reads oddly. That is a real cost of keeping the DOM honest, and it is Angular's, not the contract's.

_controlRulesDoc: How Angular spells each `control` value from a contract's `states`. THESE ARE RULES, NOT A TABLE: one entry per control value covers every state in the library. `X` is the state name in camelCase.

consumer.note: One signal input. Identical in shape to React and Vue, because there is nothing two-way about a value the user cannot change.

shared.note: ONE declaration, where React needs three props. `model()` creates the `X` input and the `XChange` output together and returns a writable signal, so a consumer writes `[(X)]` to control it, `[X]` alone to seed it, or nothing and lets the component own it. THIS IS THE SAME COLLAPSE VUE MAKES, REACHED INDEPENDENTLY — two of three backends spend one declaration on `control: shared` and the odd one out is React, whose trio is a workaround for having no two-way binding. That is the strongest evidence in the repo that ADR 0004 described the state rather than React's spelling of it.

internal.note: NO public input. The state still reaches CSS — as a native pseudo-class where the platform owns one, otherwise as a data attribute — but nothing outside can set it. Identical across all three backends.

_slotsDoc: A contract's `composition.slots` becomes CONTENT PROJECTION: `<ng-content select="[slot=x]">`, filled by a consumer writing `<span slot="label">`. Closer to Vue's named slots than to React's ReactNode props, but not the same thing — projection selects on the DOM, so the consumer supplies a real element to carry the marker, where a Vue `<template #label>` supplies none.

emits: <ng-content select="[slot=x]" /> at the part the contract names
named.note: The `slot` attribute is borrowed from the web-components idiom deliberately: it is already a standard attribute name for exactly this, so it needs no prefix and collides with nothing.

_axisOverridesDoc: Axis name -> the Angular input that carries it, for the rare case where the canonical name collides with a reserved or conventional Angular input. Empty means every axis is spelled exactly as the canon spells it, which is the desired state. Every entry needs a reason: a rename with no reason is drift with paperwork.
_behaviorBindingDoc: Behaviour vocabulary primitive -> the Angular implementation that satisfies it.
_whatAngularSuppliesThatTheOthersDoNot: Recorded because each is emitter work the other two backends need and this one does not.

suppliedByTheFramework.event handler composition: FREE, and it is the only backend where it is. Angular attaches host listeners with addEventListener rather than assigning a prop, so a consumer's own `(click)` and the component's host `(click)` BOTH fire, in DOM order, with no emitter involvement. React has to compose the chain by hand and Vue has to compose it by hand after turning attribute fallthrough off.
suppliedByTheFramework.class passthrough: The consumer writes the host element, so their `class` is simply on it. There is no passthrough to decide.
suppliedByTheFramework.reaching the host element: `inject(ElementRef)`. No template ref, no forwarded ref, no `$el`.
suppliedByTheFramework.identity attributes: A consumer cannot overwrite a host binding by writing a static attribute, because the binding is applied by the component after the template's own attributes. React had to spread props BEFORE identity attributes to get this; Vue had to disable attribute fallthrough entirely.
